full_text:
SPAIN: The SEMAF strike set for November 23 is off after a deal with the Ministry of Transport and Renfe that halts trains at risk points under red weather alerts.
SEMAF, Spain’s train drivers’ union, announced the call-off on November 20. The agreement signed in Madrid on November 19 brings together the Secretary of State for Transport and Sustainable Mobility at Spain’s Ministry of Transport and Sustainable Mobility, the management of Renfe Group and the SEMAF strike committee led by secretary general Diego Martín Fernández. It builds on the February 9, 2026 strike settlement and on a list of commitments the ministry issued on November 17. Both sides state in the document that they consider the conflict resolved.
Red weather alerts at Adif risk points
The weather protocol, agreed on November 19, is attached to the agreement as an annex. It follows a November 18 meeting at the ministry with the State Meteorological Agency (AEMET), infrastructure manager Adif, Renfe and the UGT, CCOO, SEMAF and SCF unions. When a red alert coincides with a risk point listed in Adif’s incident management manual, a list Adif updates monthly under the protocol, service on that section is suspended until the red level ends and Adif restores traffic under the conditions it sets. This applies to points classed as medium risk, high risk and signposted high risk. Until Adif finishes its annex of especially vulnerable sections, points whose risk has not yet been identified are treated the same way, with service suspended on the same two conditions.
At any alert level, a driver who reasonably perceives a serious and imminent risk reports the need to stop and halts the train at the safest available place. Train operators must pass orange and red warnings to the staff working in the affected area and time slot without delay.
AEMET currently sends Adif rain intensity forecasts every six hours, valid for 24 hours, for points on a 5-kilometer grid along the network. The annex adds 48-hour and 72-hour forecasts and 1-hour and 12-hour rainfall totals once the AEMET–Adif contract is amended. The protocol itself will keep relying on 6-hour totals, while the 1-hour and 12-hour data feed into the analysis of each weather event. Adif is to publish the AEMET bulletins on its website from November 19, and it plans to finish the list of especially vulnerable sections by year-end.
Renfe Group fleet and staffing commitments
Renfe Group will deliver a signed correction plan for technical and safety problems on Series 106, 452 and 453 trains. Each open issue gets a fixed date and a protective measure; where no interim measure controls the risk, the train stays out of service, with no automatic return when a deadline passes. The agreement also includes a plan to replace the air-conditioning on the entire public service obligation (OSP) fleet between 2027 and 2029, with €110 million earmarked for the equipment.
Candidates from Renfe’s 2026 hiring round will train for one month and then receive permanent contracts, and drivers will get two training days a year. A binding instruction, built into Renfe Group’s safety management procedures, will apply a 1990 agreement on support for staff involved in run-over incidents. Follow-up meetings take place on the first Wednesday of each month, and the State Railway Safety Agency (AESF), the Labor and Social Security Inspectorate and SEMAF will meet on the third Tuesday.
A second document lists measures completed or in progress. A guide on LZB signaling faults on high-speed lines was published on November 13. The weekly notice of temporary speed limits on conventional and meter-gauge lines will become daily. On November 17, the Council of Ministers declared urgent the processing of an amendment to the working-time rules for rail traffic staff, which still has to be adopted.

BOE, Royal Decree-Law 34/2026
The next fixed dates run from the November 20 committee meeting to the 2027 entry into force of the driving-time rule. Dates are taken from the agreement signed on November 19 and its annexes, and from Royal Decree-Law 34/2026. The May 11, 2027 date is an editorial calculation of six months from the November 11, 2026 publication. The agreement gives no date for the expanded AEMET forecasts, which depend on an amended AEMET–Adif contract.
Royal Decree-Law 34/2026 sets the driving-time rule
Several points of the agreement rest on Royal Decree-Law 34/2026 of November 10, published in the official state gazette (BOE) on November 11. It rewrites the driving-time article of Royal Decree 929/2020: every gap of less than 45 minutes between the end of a driving spell and its resumption by the same driver counts in full as driving time, even if the driver is relieved or does other work. Breaks of 45 minutes or more during tests, trial runs or inspection runs also count when staff must remain available, and in the exceptional case of a driver pair, one qualified for the vehicle and the other for the infrastructure, the time counts for both. That change takes effect six months after publication, while the rest of the decree-law applied from the day it was published.
The decree-law also rewrites Chapter IV of Title V of Rail Sector Law 38/2015, now titled “just culture,” with a new Article 71. Staff with safety duties may take necessary and proportionate measures against a serious and imminent risk, including stopping a train or not starting it. Staff who report risks or take safety decisions may not face sanctions or unfavorable treatment from their employer for doing so. The protection does not apply to intentional acts or omissions, or to gross negligence that caused foreseeable harm or seriously compromised safety, judged against the evident risk and the worker’s duties, training and means. Either case must be proven and reasoned. Reduced retirement-age coefficients are extended to staff of rail companies working on the general-interest network or interoperable lines, provided they hold one of the job categories covered by the existing scheme.
Renfe minimum services for the November 17 strike
The scale of a single strike day is set out in the minimum-services order for the November 17 strike at Renfe Group, called by SEMAF together with the Renfe Group General Committee and other unions, signed on November 12 by Secretary of State José Antonio Santano Clavero. It kept 72% of high-speed and long-distance trains, 177 of 246 affected services, against the 82% Renfe had requested. Medium-distance service was set at 65%, or 444 of 682 trains, compared with Renfe’s request for 75%, and freight at 26%, or 53 of 205 trains, against a requested 29%. Commuter trains ran at 75% at peak hours and 50% at other times outside Catalonia and the Basque Country, where the regional authorities set minimum services. The order required 4,123 workers, 30.48% of the staff called to strike.
